title: UEFA votes unanimous boycott of FIFA competitions over private equity World Cup plan
dek: All 55 UEFA member associations voted to boycott FIFA competitions, including future World Cups, if Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a stake in FIFA Forward Enterprises to a private equity group proceeds. Concacaf's 41 members also rejected the proposal. The boycott would exclude major nations including Germany, France, England, Spain, and the 2026 World Cup hosts (United States, Canada, Mexico).
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: UEFA's 55 members voted unanimously to withdraw from all FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, if the private equity proposal advances; Concacaf also rejected it on the same day.
bottom_line: The September 19 deadline for FIFA member acceptance and the September Women's U-20 World Cup offer immediate pressure points. If UEFA enforces its boycott on even one FIFA competition before the deadline, the deal's viability collapses; if FIFA moves forward regardless, the organization enters uncharted territory.
body: All 55 UEFA member associations voted to boycott FIFA competitions, including future World Cups, if Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a controlling stake in FIFA Forward Enterprises to a private equity group backed by Joshua Kushner proceeds. Over 50 UEFA members took the floor in a virtual meeting and expressed unanimity in their opposition, according to ESPN's reporting.

Concacaf, the North American confederation with 41 members, also rejected the proposal on the same day, citing lack of proper governance process and an artificially short deadline. Concacaf members include 2026 World Cup hosts the United States, Canada, and Mexico; the U.S. Soccer Federation stated on social media that it "stands with Concacaf and its members."

The boycott would affect both men's and women's World Cups, meaning world champions Spain, Germany, France, England, and every other European nation would not participate if the proposal advances. The first test of UEFA's stance will come in September when Poland is due to host the Women's U-20 World Cup.

Infantino's plan involves raising $20 billion in exchange for a private equity group gaining influence over future World Cups, including broadcasting and commercial deals. The deal would span 12 years and, according to the FIFA announcement reported by ESPN, would trigger over $80 million in payouts to each of FIFA's 211 member associations between now and 2037. Infantino set a September 19 deadline for associations to accept the plan, with a majority vote needed for implementation.

UEFA framed its position in stark terms: "Some things are simply too important to sell. The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale." The confederation cited lack of "meaningful consultation" as a further grievance, describing it as "not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football."

Concacaf's 41 members expressed deep concerns about the absence of due process, the short deadline, and lack of review by FIFA governance bodies. The confederation tasked its FIFA Council members with exploring whether existing FIFA reserves could fund FIFA Forward without private equity involvement and instructed the FIFA President to ensure any matter follows proper governance processes through the FIFA Council in accordance with FIFA Statutes.

The proposal faces resistance from three of FIFA's six continental confederations. Two critical unknowns remain unaddressed in official statements: whether FIFA would proceed with the sale even without European and North American participation, and the positions of the remaining three confederations (CONMEBOL, CAF, AFC, and OFC). A presidential election is scheduled for March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco, with a November 18 candidate declaration deadline. Infantino, who served as UEFA's general secretary before his 2016 election as FIFA president, now faces organized opposition from his former confederation.
